issues.body:
## Summary
Once [spring-projects/spring-framework#36716](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-framework/issues/36716) is resolved, Spring Boot should expose `spring.webflux.response-encoded-html-escape` as a configuration property, following the exact same pattern by which `spring.webflux.default-html-escape` was introduced in #49791 which is implemented and introduced through both spring and spring boot by me

## Background
Spring Framework PR [#36400](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-framework/pull/36400) wired `defaultHtmlEscape` into WebFlux across `WebHttpHandlerBuilder` → `HttpWebHandlerAdapter` → `ServerWebExchange`. Boot exposed that as `spring.webflux.default-html-escape` via #49791, which added a `@Nullable Boolean defaultHtmlEscape` field to `WebFluxProperties` and wired it into `HttpHandlerAutoConfiguration` via `handlerBuilder.defaultHtmlEscape(properties.getDefaultHtmlEscape())`.
Spring MVC's `RequestContext` has always had a second companion flag — `responseEncodedHtmlEscape` — that controls whether `HtmlUtils.htmlEscape(String, String)` (encoding-aware) or `HtmlUtils.htmlEscape(String)` (ISO-8859-1) is used when escaping is active. PR #36400 did not carry this flag over to WebFlux. the Framework issue [#36716](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-framework/issues/36716) I opened proposes completing that parity by adding `responseEncodedHtmlEscape` to `WebHttpHandlerBuilder`, `HttpWebHandlerAdapter`, and WebFlux `RequestContext`, mirroring the structure of #36400 exactly.

## Requested Change
Once https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-framework/issues/36716 merges, Boot should expose:

`spring.webflux.response-encoded-html-escape=true|false` 

When set to true, WebFlux `RequestContext` will call `HtmlUtils.htmlEscape(String, String)` with the response's character encoding — meaning UTF-8 applications escape only XML-significant characters (<, >, &, ") and leave non-ASCII characters like accented or Greek letters intact; when false or unset, `HtmlUtils.htmlEscape(String)` is used, which encodes all non-ASCII characters as numeric entities, a lossy default for any WebFlux application serving international content.

## Dependency
This issue is blocked on spring-projects/spring-framework#36716. No Boot-side changes are needed until that lands.

## Suggested Implementation
This follows the established pattern from #49791 precisely:

`WebFluxProperties` — add a 
```java
@Nullable Boolean responseEncodedHtmlEscape
```
 field alongside the existing `defaultHtmlEscape` field, with a matching getter and setter:
```java
/**
 * Whether response-encoded HTML escaping is enabled for the web application.
 */
private @Nullable Boolean responseEncodedHtmlEscape;
```
HttpHandlerAutoConfiguration — extend the existing properties != null block:
```java
if (properties != null) {
    handlerBuilder.defaultHtmlEscape(properties.getDefaultHtmlEscape());
    handlerBuilder.responseEncodedHtmlEscape(properties.getResponseEncodedHtmlEscape()); // added
}
```
`HttpHandlerAutoConfigurationTests` — add a `@ParameterizedTest / @ValueSource(booleans = { true, false })` test asserting that `spring.webflux.response-encoded-html-escape` propagates through the `HttpWebHandlerAdapter`, mirroring `shouldConfigureDefaultHtmlEscape()`.

The wiring target on the Framework side will be `WebHttpHandlerBuilder.responseEncodedHtmlEscape(Boolean)`, which #36716 proposes to stamp onto the exchange as `ServerWebExchange.RESPONSE_ENCODED_HTML_ESCAPE_ATTRIBUTE`, making it readable from WebFlux `RequestContext.isResponseEncodedHtmlEscape()`.

I will be happy to be assigned for this once the framework change lands
issues.title: Expose spring.webflux.response-encoded-html-escape as a Boot Configuration Property

issues.body: Boot 3.4 switched the default server shutdown to graceful, which adds the overhead of Jetty's `StatisticsHandler`. At the time, there was no other mechanism in Jetty available for graceful shutdowns. Since Jetty 12 there is a `GracefulHandler` and also `Server` implements `Graceful`. Boot could look at using those instead of `StatisticsHandler`. There might even be a `GracefulHandler` implementation that has less overhead than the one Jetty maintains, but we'd need to measure and decide if we want to maintain such a handler or use the one Jetty provides. Benchmarks show this as possibly a large effect because it does processing on every request, even if we only wanted it for shutdown.
issues.title: Use GracefulHandler rather than StatisticsHandler to coordinate graceful shutdown of Jetty

issues.body:
`EmbeddedLdapAutoConfiguration.EmbeddedLdapContextConfiguration` declares its own
`@ConditionalOnMissingBean` `LdapContextSource` and runs `before = LdapAutoConfiguration`, so
`LdapAutoConfiguration.ldapContextSource` backs off whenever embedded LDAP is active. The embedded
bean only sets `base`, `userDn`, `password` and `urls`, so everything else the client bean does is
silently dropped:

- `spring.ldap.username` / `spring.ldap.password` (replaced by `spring.ldap.embedded.credential.*`;
  if that is unset there are no credentials at all)
- `spring.ldap.anonymous-read-only`
- `spring.ldap.referral`
- `spring.ldap.base-environment.*`
- a user-provided `DirContextAuthenticationStrategy` bean

The SSL case is the most severe, as it leaves the embedded server unreachable over LDAPS. With
`spring.ldap.embedded.ssl.bundle` set, the server listens LDAPS but the auto-configured
`LdapContextSource` gets a plaintext `ldap://` URL, because its scheme comes from
`LdapProperties.determineUrls`, i.e. from the unrelated `spring.ldap.ssl.*` namespace. Setting
`spring.ldap.ssl.bundle` as well fixes the scheme but not the connection, since
`LdapAutoConfiguration.baseEnvironmentProperties` — the code that installs `LdapSslSocketFactory`
with the bundle — never runs. The handshake then fails against the JVM default trust store. There is
no property combination that yields a working client for an embedded LDAPS server today.

Background: the separate embedded bean dates back to the original LDAP auto-configuration in 1.4.0
(`6a84c369fd4`); features added to the client bean since were never mirrored. Embedded LDAPS support
(gh-48315) deliberately scoped out the client side, and gh-51382 added the client-side bundle
machinery that this fix would reuse.
issues.title: Honor spring.ldap.* properties in the Embedded LDAP server

spring-kafka is adding an opt-in container property `awaitAsyncResultsOnStop` (spring-projects/spring-kafka#4519, PR spring-projects/spring-kafka#4619, targeted at 4.2.0-M2 with backports to 4.0.x and 4.1.x, not merged yet): on container stop the in-flight async listener results (`CompletableFuture`, `Mono`, Kotlin suspend) are awaited within `shutdownTimeout` and then cancelled, so listener work no longer outlives the container and races downstream bean destruction during application shutdown. The upstream report came from production: suspend listeners writing to reactive MongoDB failed on every rolling deploy because the client was closed while they were still running.

`spring.kafka.listener.*` does not map the property, so enabling it takes a `ContainerCustomizer` bean or factory code. The reporter of the upstream issue asked for a Boot property to make adoption easier: https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-kafka/pull/4619#issuecomment-5529753812

Proposal: `spring.kafka.listener.await-async-results-on-stop` on `KafkaProperties.Listener`, mapped in `ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactoryConfigurer#configureContainer` next to the existing `immediate-stop` mapping, with the matching case in `KafkaAutoConfigurationTests`.

I'd like to do the PR for this myself once a spring-kafka release with the property is out.

issues.body:
## Motivation

Spring Boot auto-configures Actuator `HealthIndicator`s for a number of messaging and data infrastructure clients when they're on the classpath, including Redis, JDBC `DataSource`, MongoDB, Elasticsearch, and others. `PulsarAutoConfiguration` already auto-configures a `PulsarClient` and a `PulsarAdministration` bean, but there is no corresponding health indicator, so applications using `spring-boot-starter-pulsar` have no built-in way to expose the health of their Pulsar cluster through `/actuator/health`.

## Problem

Without a `PulsarHealthIndicator`, teams running Pulsar-backed services must either write their own custom `HealthIndicator`, or go without cluster-health visibility in the Actuator health endpoint, unlike users of Redis, JDBC, MongoDB, etc. This is an inconsistency in an otherwise broad set of auto-configured health indicators.

## Proposed Solution

Add a `PulsarHealthIndicator` (`org.springframework.boot.pulsar.health`) that performs a broker healthcheck through the already auto-configured `PulsarAdministration` client (`PulsarAdmin.brokers().healthcheckAsync()`, bounded by a configurable timeout), reporting `UP`/`DOWN` accordingly. Wire it up with a `PulsarHealthContributorAutoConfiguration` (`org.springframework.boot.pulsar.autoconfigure.health`), conditional on `PulsarAdministration` being on the classpath and present as a bean, and on `spring-boot-actuator` being present -- following Spring Boot's standard health-indicator auto-configuration conventions (`@ConditionalOnClass`/`@ConditionalOnBean`/`@ConditionalOnEnabledHealthIndicator("pulsar")`).

I already have a working prototype of this (indicator, auto-configuration, unit tests for the UP/DOWN/timeout cases, and documentation updates to the Pulsar reference page and the Actuator health-indicators table) and I'm happy to submit it as a PR once the general direction is confirmed by a maintainer.
issues.title: Add HealthIndicator support for Apache Pulsar

Hi team,
I've been working extensively with Spring Security recently. Countless parts of Spring Security store state—by default in memory - but many SPIs also provide SQL-backed implementations. It would be great if we could standardize these implementations and expose a consistent `initialize-schema` property for them.

Examples include:
- 
- JdbcUserDetailsManager: Stores users and their authorities in SQL (a core part of Spring Security for years).
- JdbcRegisteredClientRepository: Stores OAuth2 Authorization Server client definitions.
- JdbcOAuth2AuthorizationConsentService: Manages user consent for granted scopes.
- JdbcOAuth2AuthorizationService: Stores active OAuth2 authorizations.

We often discuss stateless APIs, but state always exists somewhere—frequently within the security context. Right now, we lack a seamless, out-of-the-box (OOTB) experience for handling that state cleanly in Spring Boot.

*Feature Request*: Could we collaborate to make the necessary updates in Spring Security so Spring Boot can, in turn, provide first-class auto-configuration and configuration properties (spring.security.*.initialize-schema) for these SQL-backed components?
issues.title: Add support for initializing the schema that Spring Security supports

issues.body: Following the change in Micrometer (https://github.com/micrometer-metrics/micrometer/issues/7312) that encourages making the active Observation LongTaskTimer in `DefaultMeterObservationHandler` opt-in instead of opt-out, it would be ideal if the Spring Boot auto-configuration and configuration properties follow suit. The history is that the relevant configuration property used to be `management.observations.long-task-timer.enabled` in Boot 3.x and was changed to `management.metrics.observations.ignored-meters` in Boot 4.0 to better align with the API in Micrometer. I'm not sure what the change should be to the configuration property, and switching from the LongTaskTimer being created by default to not being created by default will be a change in behavior for Spring Boot users. While we can't be certain about usage, we suspect that the vast majority of users are not using the `LongTaskTimer` that is being created by default now. I could not find any dashboards or alerts that are public that use it. Specifically for Spring Web MVC and WebFlux users, the templated URI path pattern is not available when the Observation is started, which means the LongTaskTimer created is tagged with `uri="UNKNOWN"`, which substantially diminishes its usefulness while still costing users overhead.
issues.title: Make the active Observation LongTaskTimer on the auto-configured DefaultMeterObservationHandler opt-in

issues.body:
**Spring Boot:** 4.2.0-M2

With `server.forward-headers-strategy=native`, a WebFlux application on Reactor Netty ignores `X-Forwarded-Prefix` in 4.2.0-M2, and theres no configuration property to enable it.

`NettyReactiveWebServerFactory` now calls `HttpServer.forwarded(useStandardHeader, useForwardedPrefix)` with `useForwardedPrefix` hard-coded to `false` (66a093dbfa, #51031).

With `X-Forwarded-Prefix: /api` and no other configuration, `ServerHttpRequest.getPath().contextPath()` is:

| Strategy | 4.1.1 | 4.2.0-M2 |
|---|---|---|
| `native` | `/api` | (empty) |
| `framework` | `/api` | (empty), can be enabled with `spring.webflux.forwarded-headers.use-forwarded-prefix=true` |

Not honoring the prefix by default matches spring-projects/spring-framework#37072, which suggests enabling it with "a separate property". However, that property only exists for the `framework` strategy. With `native`, the only options are switching strategies or writing a `NettyServerCustomizer`. The change also isnt mentioned in the 4.2.0-M1 release notes, so applications behind a proxy that sends `X-Forwarded-Prefix` will silently generate links and redirects without the prefix after upgrading.

Would you consider adding `server.netty.forwarded-headers.use-forwarded-prefix` (defaulting to `false`, like the Framework one) and passing it to `HttpServer.forwarded(...)`? Id be happy to submit a PR.
issues.title: Add support for X-Forwarded-Prefix with Reactor Netty

issues.body:
`"spring-boot-starter-test"` currently depends on `"org.skyscreamer:jsonassert"` for JSON assertions in Framework's testing support. As seen in #9248 and #41201, this is causing issues because `"org.skyscreamer:jsonassert"` depends on `"com.vaadin.external.google:android-json"` (an incomplete implementation of "org.json", according to some). This same library is declared as vulnerable in CVE-2026-110974 and no fix will be shipped. JsonAssert itself [looks abandoned at this point](https://github.com/skyscreamer/JSONassert/issues/202).

As of Spring Framework 7.1, [spring-test now supports both jsonassert and jsonunit for JSON assertions](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-framework/issues/37490). Spring Boot 4.2 projects can exclude jsonassert and import `"net.javacrumbs.json-unit:json-unit-core"` as a replacement.

We should consider making that change in the starter itself, but we need to consider that this is a breaking change: the jsonassert dependency is declared in the test compile classpath, this means that custom application tests could use jsonassert directly and switching dependency here could break their test suite.

Depending on community demand, we could consider this for 4.3.0.
issues.title: Replace JsonAssert with JsonUnit in spring-boot-starter-test

issues.body:
First of all, thank you very much for fixing #51437! The ability to require authentication for LDAP searches has made testing Active Directory integration scenarios much cleaner and closer to production behavior.

Following this, we are trying to test advanced AD edge cases—specifically mapping UPN-based bind requests (`user@domain.com`) to internal Distinguished Names using UnboundID's `InMemoryOperationInterceptor`. 

Currently, Spring Boot's auto-configured embedded LDAP server (`InMemoryDirectoryServer`) does not provide a hook to register custom `InMemoryOperationInterceptor` instances, forcing developers to either bypass the auto-configuration entirely or write custom manual test configurations.

To make the embedded LDAP support more extensible, we would like to propose two potential enhancement options:

#### Option 1: Automatic Bean Discovery (Preferred)
Automatically detect any beans implementing `InMemoryOperationInterceptor` in the application context and register them with the `InMemoryDirectoryServerConfig`. This would allow seamless dependency injection (e.g., passing resources or test data helpers into the interceptor via constructor).

#### Option 2: Configuration Property for Interceptor Class
Provide a configuration property (e.g., `spring.test.embedded.ldap.operation-interceptor`) to specify the fully qualified class name of an `InMemoryOperationInterceptor` implementation (instantiated via default constructor). 

Would you be open to adding such an extension mechanism to Spring Boot's embedded LDAP support?
issues.title: Provide customizer callback for embedded LDAP's InMemoryDirectoryServerConfig
